messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arthur was explaining French verb conjugations to a high school student at the public library when the sirens began. It was a torrential summer storm, and within minutes, a muddy wave of floodwater shattered the large ground-floor windows. He remembers the explosive sound of the glass, the immediate, foul smell of wet earth and decay, and the shock of cold water swirling around his ankles, then his knees. They were trapped for four hours before rescue teams could reach them, four hours spent in the dark after the power failed, listening to the building groan around them. The delay felt like an eternity, each passing minute a fresh confirmation that they had been forgotten and were going to die.

In the six months since the flood, the memory has refused to stay in the past. It often forces its way into his mind without warning, sometimes triggered by nothing more than the smell of damp soil after he waters the plants on his balcony. When the memory arrives, it is not just a picture; it brings with it a full-body sensation of immediate, present danger. His heart pounds, his muscles tense, and he is instantly convinced that disaster is about to strike again. This visceral feeling of imminent threat has him constantly scanning his surroundings for signs of danger, his eyes darting around any room he enters, searching for exits and assessing structural weaknesses.

This pervasive sense of being unsafe has reshaped Arthur's life. He can no longer tolerate sitting in a cafe or restaurant unless his back is firmly against a wall, allowing him a clear, unobstructed view of the entire room and all its entrances. The feeling that something terrible is happening becomes unbearable when events are delayed; if his partner is ten minutes late returning from the grocery store, his mind doesn't imagine traffic but a catastrophic car accident. To manage this constant, exhausting vigilance, Arthur has begun to systematically avoid anything he deems potentially stressful. He stopped tutoring in person, moving all his sessions online, and has declined all social invitations, believing that the only way to stay safe is to remain at home.

When an image of the water rising breaks through his defenses, so vivid he can almost feel the chill, his primary goal is to disconnect from it. He has taught himself to pretend it happened to someone else, a story he read or a movie he saw. He can recount the events in a flat, emotionless tone, as if describing a stranger's misfortune, a numbness that provides a fleeting sense of control. In the quiet moments that follow, however, his mind gets caught in loops of rumination, endlessly replaying the hours before the flood, trying to identify a different choice he could have made—leaving the library earlier, moving to a higher floor sooner—as if finding the error could somehow prevent it from ever happening again.

These strategies, designed for protection, have become a cage. His constant avoidance of the outside world has only served to reinforce his belief that it is an inherently dangerous place, making his baseline level of threat even higher. By deliberately stripping the emotion from his recall, the memory remains an unprocessed, alien fragment. This numbness means he never truly works through the horror, leaving it to ambush him later with its full sensory force. The rumination, meant to establish control, instead forces him to repeatedly visit the most terrifying moments of the trauma, keeping the memory fresh, potent, and readily accessible. The more he tries to control his experience, the more out of control he feels, and the more certain he becomes that he is living on borrowed time.

Arthur came to therapy at the urging of his partner, who could no longer watch his world shrink to the four walls of their apartment. He has lost nearly all of his students, unable to cope with the perceived stress of scheduling and deadlines. What finally broke his own resistance was realizing he could not remember the last time he had felt truly calm. He is terrified that he is losing his mind, that the danger he feels is real, and that letting his guard down for even a moment will lead to the catastrophe he is so desperate to prevent.
